newsitem.title: NIGERIA: No joy in Nigerian budget for oil joint ventures.
newsitem.headline: No joy in Nigerian budget for oil joint ventures.

text.p: Executives at Nigeria's foreign oil joint venture partners said on Monday the military government's 1997 budget was not likely to encourage oil production increases and they regretted its decision to put off privatisation.
"If the government genuinely wants us to expand production then it is going to have to allow more money for it," said an executive at one of the multinational companies who would not be named.
Another said it would be a matter of waiting to see what his own company's allocation was from the total amount before being able to tell what affect it would have in the short term.
"What really disappoints me is that there is no further statement or concrete evidence of commitment to privatisation of the upstream sector, which is the way the industry has to go," he said.
In October, finance minister Anthony Ani said Nigeria was seriously considering selling its crude oil production joint ventures and privatising oil refineries.

But in his budget broadcast on Saturday military ruler General Sani Abacha said privatisation would have to wait for further study, despite pressure from the World Bank and local business to sell off state enterprises.

In his detailed budget breakdown, Finance Minister Anthony Ani said the same $2.05 billion would be budgeted for payments to oil joint ventures as had been allocated in 1996. He also said that cash calls had been paid up to the end of 1996.
However the multinationals say they are still waiting for money from 1996.
"There are substantial payments left in both naira and dollars which run to several hundred million dollars for the companies as a whole," said one oil industry executive.
Ani on Monday projected oil production at an average 2.04 million barrels per day (bpd) in 1997, including 175,000 bpd of condensate from the Oso field.
Companies say that the previously stated goal of increasing production to 2.5 million bpd by the turn of the century could only be met with increased investment.
The five major crude oil joint ventures are run by subsidiaries of Shell, Mobil, Chevron, Agip and Elf. State-run NNPC is the majority partner in all of them.
